title: Systems Basics
whyItMatters: The intuitions that make a design answer credible: what is expensive, what races, and what is safe to retry.

questions.prompt: Order these from fastest to slowest: SSD read, main memory read, network round trip within a datacentre.
questions.explanation: Memory is around 100 nanoseconds, an SSD read tens of microseconds, and a datacentre round trip around half a millisecond.

concept.title: Numbers worth carrying
concept.summary: Orders of magnitude matter more than exact figures.
points: L1 cache: ~1ns. Main memory: ~100ns.
SSD read: ~50µs — a few hundred times slower than memory.
Same-datacentre round trip: ~0.5ms. Cross-continent: ~150ms.
The gaps vary by hardware and network, but crossing storage or network boundaries is usually orders of magnitude slower than a memory read.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for an endpoint to be idempotent?
options: It always returns the same response body
Calling it twice leaves the system in the same state as calling it once
It never writes to the database
questions.explanation: Idempotency is about resulting state, not the response. It is what makes a retry safe.

concept.title: Why retries need idempotency
concept.summary: A network timeout never tells you whether the write landed.
points: HTTP defines GET, PUT and DELETE with idempotent semantics; an implementation can still violate the contract, while POST is not idempotent by default.
A client that times out cannot know if the server committed.
An idempotency key lets the server recognise and ignore the repeat.
Without it, a retry on a payment charges twice.

questions.prompt: Two requests read a counter of 5, each add 1, and each write back. What is stored?
options: It depends on the isolation level
questions.explanation: Both read 5 and both write 6, so one increment is silently lost — the classic read-modify-write race.

concept.title: Lost update
concept.summary: The read and the write are two steps, and anything can happen between them.
points: Read-modify-write is only safe if the pair is atomic.
An atomic increment in the database avoids the round trip entirely.
Optimistic locking adds a version check on write and retries on conflict.
Pessimistic locking takes the row lock up front and blocks the other writer.

questions.prompt: When is optimistic locking the better choice?
options: When conflicts are rare and you would rather not hold locks
When the write must never be retried
When the table has no primary key
questions.explanation: Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare and pays only when one happens; under contention its retries cost more than a lock would.

concept.title: Two ways to not lose a write
concept.summary: Pick by how often you expect to collide.
points: Optimistic: check a version on write, retry on mismatch. No lock held.
Pessimistic: lock the row first. Nobody else proceeds until you commit.
Rare conflicts favour optimistic; heavy contention favours pessimistic.
Holding a lock across a network call is how deadlocks and timeouts start.

options: A cache growing past its memory limit
Many requests all missing the same expired key at once and hitting the origin together
Two caches disagreeing about a value
A cache serving data that was never written
questions.explanation: One popular key expiring can send every concurrent request through to the origin at the same instant.

concept.title: The moment a hot key expires
concept.summary: Expiry is synchronised, and that is the problem.
points: All in-flight requests miss simultaneously and pile onto the origin.
A lock or single-flight lets one request refill while others wait.
stale-while-revalidate serves the old value during the refill.
Jittered TTLs stop many keys expiring on the same tick.

questions.prompt: Why does putting a CDN in front of an app make it feel faster, even when the server was never slow?
expects: names physical distance and round-trip latency
distinguishes server processing time from transit time
mentions caching at the edge or connection termination
questions.probeIfMissing: How long does a packet take to cross an ocean, and how many times does a page load do it?

concept.title: Distance is the slow part
concept.summary: You cannot optimise your way past the speed of light.
points: A cross-continent round trip is ~150ms, and a page makes many.
TLS and TCP handshakes each cost round trips before any data moves.
An edge node terminates those close to the user, even for uncached responses.
Cached assets never reach your origin at all.

questions.prompt: One in fifty requests fails, and you cannot reproduce it locally. How do you chase it?
expects: reaches for logs, tracing or metrics rather than local reproduction
looks for what differs between the failing and passing requests
names a plausible intermittent cause such as a race, a timeout or one bad instance
questions.probeIfMissing: What do the failing requests have in common that the others do not?

concept.title: Chasing the intermittent
concept.summary: A 2% failure rate is a pattern, not randomness. Find the axis.
points: Group failures by instance, region, user and time — one axis usually stands out.
One bad instance behind a load balancer produces exactly this shape.
A timeout just under the norm fails only the slow tail.
A race fails only when two requests interleave, so load is the trigger.

questions.prompt: A service is struggling, so clients retry failed calls. Why can that make things worse?
expects: describes retries adding load to an already-loaded service
names synchronised retries or a retry storm
reaches for backoff, jitter or a circuit breaker
questions.probeIfMissing: What happens to total traffic the moment every client retries at once?

concept.title: Retries amplify
concept.summary: The naive retry multiplies load exactly when the service can least take it.
points: Every client retrying triples traffic against a service already failing.
Fixed-interval retries synchronise into waves.
Exponential backoff with jitter spreads them out.
A circuit breaker stops calling a dead dependency at all until it recovers.
